rationale: B wins because it refuses to launder the weakest causal claim. Its headline, "Chipotle won't raise prices this year — but won't say if the robots are why," is the skeptical spine a reporter can actually use, while A opens with "Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" and later claims "Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices." A has richer beat packaging, but those two overclaims are exactly how a decent angle gets turned into a credibility problem.
gaps_in_A: "Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices" is not in the update. Chipotle said prices will stay flat and Autocado is rolling out; it did not say robots justify the price decision.
"Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" overstates an implied causal link the set itself later admits is unproven. The caveat is good; the headline ignores it.
"Its Competitors Are Taking Notes" invents competitor attention. No competitor reaction or adoption signal appears in the facts.
The pricing angle and investor-margin angle partly duplicate the same unsupported automation-pays-for-price-freeze thesis, just aimed at different desks.
gaps_in_B: "call it a pilot, not a rollout" is a little too cute. The supplied fact says 100 restaurants are a rollout; the stronger frame is scale skepticism, not relabeling the fact.
"making the two-system pattern visible for the first time" invents timing. The update says Digital Makeline is also being tested, not that this is the first disclosure.
"In Chipotle's test kitchens, one robot cut guacamole prep time in half" is thin as a standalone story. That metric is better proof inside the pricing, labor, or operations angle.
"No clean hand-off yet" is too frozen. You can still run journalist-fit-check against QSR finance, labor, and restaurant-tech reporters while the proof gaps are being closed.
